The plan is clear and honest about its gaps, but several changes would make the written submission much more persuasive.

1) Replace weak validation with hard evidence. Fourteen conversations and informal tests at two practices are anecdotal. Report specifics: how many coaches said they would pay, at what price, and whether any signed a letter of intent or put down a deposit. Quantify prototype results (number of players, catches recorded, whether glove scores matched coach judgment, whether scores changed after the suggested drills). The central claim is that the score is accurate and drives improvement, so evidence for that should be the centerpiece.

2) Validate or defend the scoring methodology. The score rests on rules from two coaches, not data. Explain how you will validate it: compare glove scores to expert video review, collect a labeled dataset in the pilot, and show reliability across ages and ball sizes. Without this, a skeptical judge will question whether the product measures what it claims.

3) Fix the market sizing. A top-down TAM of over $1B from players times an assumed price is the weak approach you acknowledge yourselves. Lead with a bottom-up SAM: 20-30K programs, a realistic share of those that buy, and the price. Cite the sources for player and team counts. Show how many programs you can reach in your region in years one to three, and how you derived the year-three $300K+ figure (units, price, churn, conversion). Right now projections appear as a bare number.

4) Tighten unit economics and pricing logic. A $38 prototype parts cost against a $450 six-glove kit (about $75 per glove) leaves thin margin once you add assembly, battery packs, packaging, shipping, returns, app development and support, and the wired battery pack will not survive real practice use. Provide a rough BOM, a target cost at volume, and gross margin by channel. Also address durability and washability, since gloves are used by kids in rain and mud, and replacement and warranty costs. Justify why a team would renew a $120 subscription after year one.

5) Clarify the buyer and the go-to-market. Most rec-league coaches are volunteers with tiny budgets, and leagues, not coaches, often control purchasing. Identify who writes the check (league, booster club, school athletic department, parents) and how long the sales cycle is. A six-glove kit for a whole roster implies receivers rotate gloves; explain how that works in practice. Name concrete channels such as league associations, Pop Warner or USA Football affiliates, and school district purchasing.

6) Address risks head on: data privacy and child safety (collecting biometric-style data on minors, COPPA and parental consent), fit and safety of embedded electronics, and compliance with league equipment rules. Also address the real alternative that coaches already use free YouTube drills or phone video, so explain why the glove beats a phone camera plus coaching content.

7) Strengthen the competition section. Name actual competitors and adjacent products (smart-ball makers, wearable sensor and video-analysis companies, receiver training gloves and apps) and show a comparison table on price, data captured, and ease of use. 'We are not aware of a product' reads as under-researched. Put the IP gap in context with a prior-art search and a clearer defensibility story, since price and simplicity alone are easy to copy.

8) Show a credible team plan. The team is strong on enthusiasm but lacks manufacturing and sports-industry experience, and is student-based, so also address availability after graduation. Name specific advisors you are pursuing and why, and state who owns which deliverables in the 12-month plan.

9) Make the funding ask more concrete. Break the $25,000 into line items (parts and tooling for 20 gloves, wireless redesign, pilot logistics, patent and legal) and tie each to a milestone with measurable success criteria, such as pilot teams retained, score validation accuracy, cost-per-unit target and number of paid pilots. Include a month-by-month timeline and what the funding gets you to next (a follow-on raise, pre-orders).

10) Tighten presentation. Open with the single most compelling proof point, cut hedging language ('we think', 'we believe'), fix typos such as 'embeded', add a product image or diagram, and include a simple financial table (revenue, costs, cash burn by quarter) instead of prose. Reframe projections as scenarios (conservative, base, upside) with stated assumptions so the numbers are testable rather than speculative.
